plan.angle: Same framework, but source-tag the tips to the verified 2026 DMSO review and the expert consensus statements, not the unverified NCP October 2026 review. Slide 3 uses one named trial with its population, timeframe and placebo rate. The habits are: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping at comfortably full, fewer high-fat or greasy meals, fluids, and gradual fibre. That's six, to match the title. Keep the red-flag slide and a no-dose prescriber slide. Title: 'GLP-1 Nausea & Constipation: 6 Habits Expert Reviews Say Can Help'.

plan.why: A high-volume evergreen question refreshed with a citable October 2026 review. The petrelintide 'fewer side effects' news keeps GI tolerability topical, and a checklist format gets saved. | fact-check: I couldn't verify the cited source. I found no 'Nutrition in Clinical Practice, Oct 2026' expert review of GI side effects. The nearest NCP item (doi 10.1002/ncp.70172) appears to be a narrative review of GLP-1 RA effects on nutrient intake. Its date and scope couldn't be confirmed (the page returned a 403). Don't build the carousel on it unless the writer confirms the exact title, date and that it covers these tips. Verified alternatives that support the same habits: (1) the 2026 Dove Press DMSO review 'Gastrointestinal Adverse Effects of GLP-1 and Dual GLP-1/GIP Receptor Agonists'. It recommends smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding high-fat or spicy foods, stopping at early fullness, and adequate fluids and fibre. It notes GI effects are mostly mild to moderate, dose-dependent and transient. (2) The 2022 multidisciplinary expert consensus on managing GI adverse events (PMC9821052). (3) The expert Delphi consensus on nutritional and lifestyle supportive care (PMC12768930). For slide 3, use one named trial with its placebo rate, e.g. STEP 1, semaglutide 2.4 mg, adults with overweight or obesity without diabetes, 68 weeks: nausea 44% vs 17% on placebo, constipation 24% vs 11%. Verify these against the NEJM paper, and don't pool figures from different trials. Make the habit count in the title match the slides exactly. Keep slide 8 to 'your prescriber can adjust your plan', with no dose-reduction or re-titration wording, even though the reviews mention it. Verified sources: https://www.dovepress.com/gastrointestinal-adverse-effects-of-glp-1-and-dual-glp-1gip-receptor-a-peer-reviewed-fulltext-article-DMSO ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9821052/ ; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12768930/

package.title: GLP-1 Nausea & Constipation: 6 Habits Expert Reviews Say Can Help

social.facebook_caption:
Dealing with nausea or constipation on a GLP-1 medicine? A 2026 review found these GI effects are usually mild to moderate, dose-dependent, and often temporary.

Six habits reviews point to: smaller, more frequent meals; eating slowly; stopping at the first sign of fullness; going easy on greasy or fried food; sipping fluids through the day (unless you've been told to limit fluids); and building up fiber gradually. In the STEP 1 trial (adults with overweight or obesity, no diabetes), 44.2% on semaglutide reported nausea (vs 17.4% on placebo) and 23.4% reported constipation (vs 9.5%) over 68 weeks; most effects were mild to moderate, and 4.5% stopped due to GI effects vs 0.8% on placebo.

If you get severe belly pain, can't keep fluids down, or notice signs of dehydration, contact a clinician promptly.

factcheck.summary: The carousel is accurate and safe. The DMSO 2026 review (Yılmaz & Bastemir, vol 19, published 30 Jan 2026) says GI effects are generally dose-dependent and temporary. It recommends smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding high-fat food, stopping at early fullness, drinking enough and getting enough fiber, and it describes slower stomach emptying as the cause. The J Clin Med consensus (online Dec 2022, issue 12(1) 2023, so the 2023 issue year is correct) says the same about eating slowly, smaller portions, stopping when full, low-fat meals, fluids and fiber. The STEP 1 figures match the published trial: nausea 44.2% vs 17.4%, constipation 23.4% vs 9.5%, any GI event 74.2% vs 47.9%, and stopping because of GI effects 4.5% vs 0.8%. The population, the 68-week timeframe and the placebo comparator are all stated. The NEJM page blocks automated fetching (403), but the article exists, and the numbers and the 'mostly mild to moderate' wording agree with the trial report. The NHS pages back up the red flags: pancreatitis pain in the stomach or back that won't go away, gallstone pain with a high temperature or yellow skin, and dehydration signs such as dizziness and peeing less. The last-reviewed dates are correct. The title's promise of 6 habits is kept, the prescriber line is there, and there are no dosing or medication-change instructions. Three small wording fixes are listed below; none of them blocks publication.

issues.claim: Can't keep fluids down — Repeated vomiting
issues.problem: This red flag isn't stated in any cited NHS page I could confirm. The dehydration page only says to start with small sips if you're being sick. The semaglutide page lists pancreatitis, not ongoing vomiting. It's clinically sensible, but the source tag doesn't clearly cover it.
issues.fix: Change the detail to: "Repeated vomiting, can't keep fluids down" and change the slide body to: "These can signal problems such as pancreatitis, gallbladder trouble or dehydration. If sickness or other side effects don't go away, get medical help promptly. Sources: NHS semaglutide; NHS gallstones; NHS dehydration."

issues.problem: The bubble is accurate (4.5% < 5%) but drops the placebo comparator, so on its own it plays down the 4.5% vs 0.8% gap.
issues.fix: Replace the bubble with: "Under 1 in 20 stopped (vs under 1 in 100 on placebo)"

issues.problem: General fluid advice with no caveat for people told to limit fluids (heart failure, advanced kidney disease).
issues.fix: Change the detail to: "Drink enough through the day (unless you've been told to limit fluids)"
